title: The Projection Pipeline: projCoeff → orthProj → orthResidual
content: The three definitions form a clean pipeline: `projCoeff v u = ⟪v,u⟫/⟪v,v⟫` is the scalar coefficient of the projection; `orthProj v u = projCoeff v u • v` is the projection vector itself; `orthResidual v u = u - orthProj v u` is the component of u orthogonal to v. The fundamental theorem `orthResidual_inner_eq_zero` proves ⟪orthResidual v u, v⟫ = 0 by `field_simp; ring` after expanding the inner product. The decomposition identity u = orthProj v u + orthResidual v u holds trivially.
mathContext: For an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ (real or complex), the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto $v \ne 0$ is $\text{proj}_v(u) = \frac{\langle v, u\rangle}{\langle v, v\rangle} v$. The residual $u - \text{proj}_v(u)$ is orthogonal to $v$: $\langle u - \text{proj}_v(u), v\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle - \frac{\langle v, u\rangle}{\langle v, v\rangle}\langle v, v\rangle = \langle u,v\rangle - \langle v, u\rangle = 0$ (using conjugate symmetry $\langle v,u\rangle = \overline{\langle u,v\rangle}$ — the `inner_conj_symm` Mathlib lemma). The `field_simp; ring` proof works because Lean can simplify the division after establishing $\langle v,v\rangle \ne 0$.

title: Two-Vector Gram-Schmidt: Orthogonality by Residual
content: The two-vector Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization is just the residual computation: given v₁ ≠ 0 and u₂, set v₂ = orthResidual v₁ u₂ = u₂ - (⟪v₁,u₂⟫/⟪v₁,v₁⟫)·v₁. Then v₂ ⊥ v₁ by `orthResidual_inner_eq_zero`. The theorem `gramSchmidt2_pair_orthogonal` gets ⟪v₁, v₂⟫ = 0 from ⟪v₂, v₁⟫ = 0 using `inner_eq_zero_symm`. This is the complete 2-vector Gram-Schmidt: no computation needed beyond the fundamental orthogonality of the residual.
mathContext: Gram-Schmidt (2-vector): Given $v_1, u_2$ with $v_1 \ne 0$, set $v_2 = u_2 - \frac{\langle v_1, u_2\rangle}{\langle v_1, v_1\rangle} v_1$. Then $v_1 \perp v_2$: $\langle v_2, v_1\rangle = \langle u_2 - \text{proj}_{v_1}(u_2), v_1\rangle = 0$. The symmetric form $\langle v_1, v_2\rangle = 0$ follows from $\langle x, y\rangle = 0 \Leftrightarrow \langle y, x\rangle = 0$ (which holds because $\langle y,x\rangle = \overline{\langle x,y\rangle}$ and $\overline{0} = 0$).

title: Three-Vector Gram-Schmidt: The Cross-Term Cancellation
content: The 3-vector step `gramSchmidt3 v₁ v₂ u₃ = orthResidual v₂ (orthResidual v₁ u₃)` first removes the v₁-component of u₃, then removes the v₂-component. Orthogonality to v₂ is immediate (it's the final residual). Orthogonality to v₁ requires the key assumption v₁ ⊥ v₂: when computing ⟪gramSchmidt3 v₁ v₂ u₃, v₁⟫, expanding produces a term `(⟪v₂, ...⟫/⟪v₂,v₂⟫)·⟪v₂, v₁⟫`. This cross-term vanishes because ⟪v₂, v₁⟫ = conj(⟪v₁, v₂⟫) = conj(0) = 0.
mathContext: The key algebraic fact: $\langle \text{GS}_3(v_1,v_2,u_3), v_1 \rangle = \langle u_3 - \text{proj}_{v_1}(u_3) - \text{proj}_{v_2}(u_3 - \text{proj}_{v_1}(u_3)), v_1 \rangle$. After expanding: $\langle u_3, v_1\rangle - \frac{\langle v_1,u_3\rangle}{\langle v_1,v_1\rangle}\langle v_1,v_1\rangle - \frac{\langle v_2, u_3 - \ldots\rangle}{\langle v_2,v_2\rangle} \cdot \underbrace{\langle v_2, v_1\rangle}_{= 0} = 0$. Without $v_1 \perp v_2$, the last term would NOT vanish. This is why Gram-Schmidt processes the orthogonalized vectors in order — each new projection must be against already-orthogonalized vectors.

title: CS Equality ↔ Residual Zero: The Central Biconditional
content: The theorem `cs_equality_iff_residual_zero` proves: ‖⟪u,v⟫‖ = ‖u‖·‖v‖ ↔ orthResidual v u = 0. The backward direction (scalar multiple → equality) is a direct computation. The forward direction uses the Pythagorean decomposition: ‖u‖² = ‖residual‖² + ‖projection‖². From CS equality, one derives ‖projection‖ = ‖u‖, forcing ‖residual‖ = 0. The proof uses `orthResidual_eq_zero_iff_smul` to convert 'residual = 0' to '∃ c, u = c·v'.
mathContext: The proof reconstructs the CS equality proof from scratch using the projection decomposition. Let $c = \langle v,u\rangle/\langle v,v\rangle$ and $w = u - cv$. Then: (1) $w \perp v$ so $w \perp cv$, giving Pythagoras $\|u\|^2 = \|w\|^2 + \|cv\|^2$; (2) $|\langle u,v\rangle| = \|cv\|\cdot\|v\| = \|c\|\cdot\|v\|^2$; (3) CS equality forces $\|c\|\cdot\|v\| = \|u\|$, so $\|cv\|^2 = \|u\|^2$, so $\|w\|^2 = 0$, so $w = 0$. The forward direction (residual zero → CS equality) is simply: if $u = cv$ then $|\langle u,v\rangle| = |c|\cdot\|v\|^2 = \|cv\|\cdot\|v\| = \|u\|\cdot\|v\|$.

title: Norm Bound: Projection Decreases Norm via Pythagoras
content: The theorem `norm_orthResidual_le` proves ‖orthResidual v u‖ ≤ ‖u‖ using the Pythagorean theorem. Since residual ⊥ projection, we have ‖u‖² = ‖residual‖² + ‖projection‖². Since ‖projection‖² ≥ 0, we get ‖residual‖² ≤ ‖u‖². The proof uses `orthResidual_inner_eq_zero` to get the perpendicularity, then `norm_add_sq` (with the appropriate sign convention) to get the Pythagorean identity, and finally `nlinarith` to conclude.
mathContext: Key geometric fact: Orthogonal projection is the closest point in a subspace. $\|u - \text{proj}_v(u)\| \le \|u - w\|$ for any $w$ in span$(v)$. In particular, ‖residual‖ ≤ ‖u‖ (choosing $w = 0$). The formal Pythagorean identity: if $x \perp y$ then $\|x+y\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2$. This is `norm_add_sq (𝕜 := 𝕜)` after verifying $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ forces the cross-term $\text{Re}(\langle x,y\rangle) = 0$ in the Mathlib expansion $\|x+y\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2 + 2\text{Re}(\langle x,y\rangle)$.
